doc.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Replacing Ray Pirello and first night with the Basie band
summary: He explains how he filled in for the injured new drummer, got the job, the three bass players named John, and joining with no rehearsal.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: So you played some with the Basie band?
Tell us about that rhythm section, that Kansas City sound. That was different than the east coast or the west coast, that midwest kind of swing.
Who did you follow into, I mean who was the drummer before you?

Well it’s an interesting story. A young man had been hired by Basie by the name of [sounds like] Ray Pirello. And he’d just been with the band a few weeks when he was in a very bad car accident in Chicago and wound up in the hospital. And Basic called me to come fill in, which I did. Originally I think it was one of these week to ten day things, until Ray was better. But his injuries were more extensive than anybody thought. And by the time Ray was well and absolutely fit and ready to go again I’d been with the band about maybe a month and a half or two months, and I was starting to get a little bit of newspaper notice, which never hurts. And so the Basie gave me the job. Now here’s the weird thing. Okay, Ray was with the band for a couple of weeks and I jumped in. Then at one point we were playing with Sammy Davis Jr. we were down in Florida, down in Miami Beach, and my dear friend Duffy Jackson was working with Sammy. Then, after I left the Basie band, Duffy joined Basie and Ray went with Sammy. So it was like —

Yeah, the same people, and that worked out really good. But the Basie rhythm section, that’s one humongous responsibility to think about because, and I love being here with this jazz festival with John Heard because when I was on the band, four and a half years, we had three bass players. They were all named John: it was John Heard, John Duke and John Clayton. And John Heard left the band for a while and John Duke came in. John Duke left the band and John Heard came back. Then John left the band and Clayton came in. So it was so much that Bobby Plater, one of the writers of a wonderful tune musical called “Jersey Bounce,” wrote a special solo for John Clayton called John the Third, naturally. But when I first started with the Basie band it was John Duke, myself, and of course Freddie Green, Count Basie. And it was, oh, I can’t believe that I didn’t actually maybe go slightly insane the first time I sat down to work with the Basie band because the responsibility of the drum chair in that band is enormous. But I was young and foolish and I was scared to death, absolutely just frightened to death, because there was no rehearsal, no tryout. Basie called me on a Tuesday morning, I jumped on a plane and flew to Chicago, somehow got my drums and everything down to the Happy Medium — which later became the Jazz Showcase up on Rush Street, and is now in a different

location in Chicago — checked into the hotel, had something to eat, met with Mr. Basie, and showed up for work. And that was it. Well you see, one of the wonderful things about something like that is that the leader of the band or the band itself will find out real fast if you can play, and real fast if you can’t. You know there’s no if. I mean you’re not hanging around for six months until someone says “well I don’t think he’s making it.” You know it’s phew, it’s real quick.
